title: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
summary: Why thread-per-connection and select or poll stop scaling, how epoll's interest and ready lists work, level versus edge triggering, and how libuv-style loops add timers and thread pools.
outcomes: Explain why thread-per-connection and busy-polling waste resources on mostly idle connections
Compute the per-call cost of select and poll versus epoll_wait for n watched and k ready descriptors
Trace how a packet moves a socket onto epoll's ready list and out through epoll_wait
Write correct edge-triggered code that drains to EAGAIN, and spot level-triggered EPOLLOUT spins
Predict event loop latency when callbacks block, and decide what belongs on a thread pool

lessons.title: Why one thread per connection stops scaling

blocks.md:
A network server spends most of its life waiting. A chat client sends a message every few seconds, a browser keeps an idle keep-alive connection open, a slow phone uploads a request over a bad link. Each connection is a **socket**, which the program sees as a file descriptor (a small integer such as 5).

By default `read` on a socket is **blocking**: if no bytes have arrived, the kernel puts the calling thread to sleep until some do. That makes the simplest server design obvious: accept a connection, start a thread for it, and let that thread call `read`, handle the request, `write` the reply and loop.

Thread-per-connection is easy to write because each thread's code is a straight line, and the OS scheduler gives every client a fair turn. The cost shows up when connections are many and mostly idle. Each thread is a kernel task with its own stack (under glibc the default stack size comes from the `RLIMIT_STACK` limit, or 2 MB on most architectures when that limit is unlimited, per [pthread_create(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_create.3.html)), and every hand-off between threads is a context switch, which you met in the prerequisite course.

Dan Kegel's page on the **C10K problem** asked exactly this: how should one server handle ten thousand clients at once, when the hardware clearly could?

blocks.title: Three clients over 100 ms: three threads versus one loop

scenes.caption: Thread-per-connection: each client gets a thread. Data for A, B and C arrives at 10, 40 and 70 ms, and each request takes 2 ms of CPU. The rest of the time every thread sleeps inside read.
Event loop: one thread asks the kernel to wait on all three sockets at once, then runs a short handler for whichever socket is ready. Same work, one thread.
Side by side: the loop thread is busy for 6 ms out of 100 (6 percent). The three-thread design does the same 6 ms of work but keeps three sleeping threads, and at 10,000 clients it keeps 10,000.

blocks.md: The first idea for using one thread is **nonblocking I/O**. Set the `O_NONBLOCK` flag on each socket and `read` never sleeps: if no data is queued it fails at once with the error `EAGAIN` (also spelled `EWOULDBLOCK`). Then loop over every socket and try to read from each one.

blocks.prompt: A naive single-thread server keeps 10,000 nonblocking sockets and calls read on each of them in turn. Right now 5 of them have data. How many system calls does one pass make, and what happens when no client sends anything for a minute?
blocks.reveal:
One pass makes **10,000** `read` calls, and **9,995** of them fail with `EAGAIN`. When nobody sends anything, the loop keeps spinning through all 10,000 sockets, burning a full CPU core to learn nothing.

What is missing is a way to ask the kernel *which* sockets can make progress, and to sleep until at least one can.

blocks.title: System calls per pass with 10,000 connections

scenes.caption: 5 sockets have data. Spinning costs 10,000 reads. Asking the kernel first costs 1 wait call plus 5 reads, so 6 system calls.
500 sockets have data. Spinning still costs 10,000. Asking first costs 1 plus 500, so 501: the work now follows the number of active sockets, not the number of open ones.

blocks.md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

Linux has three readiness interfaces. `select` and `poll` are old and portable; **epoll** is Linux specific, added in kernel 2.5.44, and designed to scale to large numbers of watched descriptors. Other systems have their own: FreeBSD and macOS have `kqueue`, Solaris had `/dev/poll` and event ports. The next lesson shows why `select` and `poll` were not enough.

Readiness is a hint, not a promise. The [select(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/select.2.html) page warns that a socket can be reported readable and a following read can still block, for example when the arrived packet had a bad checksum and was dropped. That is why event loops always use nonblocking sockets.

blocks.question: A server handles 20,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections with one thread per connection. Which cost grows directly with the number of *idle* connections?
options: CPU time spent parsing requests
A sleeping thread, with its own stack and kernel task, for every connection
Network bandwidth used by the replies
The number of bytes each request contains
blocks.explain: Parsing and bandwidth scale with *active* traffic. An idle connection does no work, but in thread-per-connection it still owns a whole thread: a stack, a kernel task, and a place in the scheduler. An event loop keeps only a small per-connection record instead.

blocks.question: Why do event loops set O_NONBLOCK on every socket even though they only read sockets the kernel reported as ready?
options: Because epoll refuses to watch blocking sockets
Because nonblocking reads are faster to copy
Because readiness can be spurious, and one blocking read would stall every other client on the loop
Because blocking sockets cannot be written to
blocks.explain: epoll watches blocking sockets just fine. But a readiness report is only a hint: the data may have been discarded, or another thread may have consumed it. With a blocking socket that read would put the only loop thread to sleep, and every other connection would wait with it.

lessons.title: select and poll: readiness that costs O(n) per call

blocks.md: `select(nfds, readfds, writefds, exceptfds, timeout)` takes three **fd_sets**. An fd_set is a bitmap: bit *i* set means "watch descriptor *i*". `nfds` is the highest descriptor you care about plus one, so the kernel knows how many bits to look at. On return, the kernel **overwrites** each set so that only the ready descriptors keep their bit. The man page calls this value-result design an error: because your input is destroyed, you must rebuild every set before each call.

blocks.title: One select call on a 16-bit readfds

scenes.caption: Before the call: the program sets bits 3, 5, 8 and 12 (four sockets) and passes nfds = 13, one more than the highest descriptor.
Inside the kernel: it walks every bit from 0 to 12 and asks each watched file whether it is readable. The work follows nfds, not the number of ready sockets.
On return: only socket 8 had data, so select returns 1 and the set now holds a single bit. The record of what you were watching is gone.
Before the next call the program must set bits 3, 5, 8 and 12 again. A server watching thousands of sockets rebuilds and re-sends the whole bitmap on every loop iteration.

blocks.md: glibc fixes `FD_SETSIZE` at **1024**, and passing a descriptor of 1024 or higher to the `FD_SET` macros is undefined behavior. A busy server easily has descriptors above 1023, so select silently corrupts memory there. The man page says all modern applications should use poll or epoll instead.

`poll(fds, nfds, timeout)` replaces bitmaps with an array of `struct pollfd { int fd; short events; short revents; }`, 8 bytes each. You fill `events`, the kernel fills `revents`, so the input survives and there is no 1024 limit.

The cost per call is still linear. Reading the kernel's `fs/select.c`, one `poll` call copies the whole array into the kernel, calls the poll check of **every** entry, and, if nothing is ready, adds the thread to the wait queue (the kernel's per-file list of sleepers to wake when its state changes) of every one of the files before sleeping. On return it writes `revents` back for every entry. Nothing is remembered between calls.
Write $n$ for the number of watched descriptors and $k$ for how many are ready on a given call. A busy server has large $n$ but, at any instant, small $k$: most connections are idle.

blocks.caption: Per-call work. poll pays for every watched descriptor on every call. epoll (next lesson) pays for registration once, then each wait pays only for the ready ones.

scenes.caption: 1 in 1,000 connections is ready per call. At 10,000 connections poll examines 10,000 entries; epoll_wait hands back 10. Simplified model: it counts entries, not nanoseconds.
10 percent ready: the gap shrinks to 10x. The more connections are active at once, the less a ready list saves.
Everything ready on every call: the two curves meet. With few or always-busy descriptors poll is not slower in this model, and epoll adds an epoll_ctl system call for every change of interest.

blocks.prompt: A server polls 10,000 sockets and 5 are ready. How many bytes does one poll call copy into the kernel, and how many bytes of results does epoll_wait copy out for the same 5 ready sockets on x86-64?
blocks.reveal:
poll copies the full array in: 10,000 x 8 bytes = **80,000 bytes**, then writes `revents` back for all 10,000 entries.

`epoll_wait` copies out only the ready events. The kernel's `struct epoll_event` is a 4-byte event mask plus an 8-byte data field, packed to **12 bytes** on x86-64, so 5 events are **60 bytes**. The interest set never crosses the boundary again after `epoll_ctl` registered it.

blocks.question: A server uses select and keeps a single fd_set variable that it fills once at startup and passes to every call. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, select remembers the interest set inside the kernel
After the first return the set holds only the ready descriptors, so later calls stop watching the others
select returns EINVAL because the set is reused
The kernel doubles the set size on each call
blocks.explain: fd_sets are value-result arguments: select overwrites them with the ready subset. Reusing the same variable means each call watches only what was ready last time, and idle connections silently drop out. You must copy the master set before every call, which is part of why per-call cost is O(n).

blocks.question: A proxy holds 50,000 mostly idle connections and wakes about 1,000 times per second. Which change cuts per-wakeup kernel work the most?
options: Switch from poll to select
Raise FD_SETSIZE to 65536 and keep select
Move to epoll so the kernel keeps the interest set and returns only ready descriptors
Call poll with a timeout of 0
blocks.explain: With poll every wakeup copies and scans 50,000 entries, so the scan repeats 1,000 times a second. epoll stores the interest set in the kernel once and each wait touches only ready items. select is worse (bitmap rebuilds, 1024 limit), and a zero timeout only turns waiting into spinning.

lessons.title: Inside epoll: interest list, ready list, epoll_wait

blocks.md:
Three system calls manage it:

1. `epoll_create1(0)` creates an instance and returns its descriptor.
2. `epoll_ctl(epfd, op, fd, &ev)` with `op` = `EPOLL_CTL_ADD`, `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` or `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` edits the interest list. `ev.events` is a bit mask such as `EPOLLIN` (readable) or `EPOLLOUT` (writable); `ev.data` is 8 bytes the kernel stores and hands back untouched, usually a pointer to your connection struct.
3. `epoll_wait(epfd, events, maxevents, timeout)` blocks until something is on the ready list, then copies up to `maxevents` entries into your array. `timeout` is in milliseconds: -1 waits forever, 0 returns immediately.

scenes.caption: epoll_ctl ADD registers sockets 5, 6 and 7. Each becomes an entry in the interest list, and epoll hooks a callback onto each socket's wait queue (dashed). This is paid once per socket, not per wait.
The thread calls epoll_wait. The ready list is empty, so the thread sleeps. No socket is scanned while it sleeps.
A packet arrives for socket 6. The network stack wakes the socket's wait queue, which runs epoll's callback: it appends socket 6 to the ready list and wakes the sleeping thread.
epoll_wait copies the one ready entry (events = EPOLLIN, plus the stored data field) to user space and returns 1. The other two sockets cost nothing.

Data arrives on sockets 5 and 7 together. Both callbacks queue entries. A call with maxevents = 1 returns one of them; the next call returns the other, because epoll_wait round-robins through ready items that do not fit.

blocks.md:
The diagram follows the kernel source, [fs/eventpoll.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/fs/eventpoll.c): each instance holds a red-black tree of `epitem` structs (the interest list, keyed by the descriptor and its open file) and a linked list `rdllist` (the ready list). `ep_poll_callback` runs when a watched file wakes its waiters and links the item onto the ready list. `epoll_wait` re-checks each item on that list and copies out the ones that still have events.

That is the whole trick: the expensive part, noticing readiness, happens at the moment a socket's state changes, driven by the device, instead of the waiting thread scanning everything.

blocks.caption: Storing a pointer in data lets the loop find its per-connection state with no lookup. EPOLLERR and EPOLLHUP are always reported, even if you did not ask for them.

blocks.title: A tiny epoll server, step by step

scenes.caption: Setup. A fresh process has descriptors 0 to 2, the listening socket got 3, so the epoll instance gets 4. The listening socket is registered for EPOLLIN, which fires when a connection is waiting.
The loop blocks in epoll_wait with timeout -1. A client connects, the listener becomes readable, and the call returns 1.
The ready descriptor is the listener, so accept4 takes the new connection and makes it nonblocking in the same call. It gets descriptor 5, the lowest free number.
The new socket joins the interest list. From now on the kernel watches it with no further work from the loop.
Back in epoll_wait. Client 5 sends 100 bytes and a second client connects in the same instant, so one call returns 2 events.
Event 0 is socket 5: read returns the 100 queued bytes and the handler runs. A return of 0 would mean the peer closed.
Event 1 is the listener again: the second client is accepted as descriptor 6 and registered. One wakeup served two unrelated events.

blocks.md: epoll cannot help with disk files. `epoll_ctl` fails with `EPERM` for a regular file or directory, and poll reports such files as always ready, because a disk read never becomes "ready" in advance: it just has to wait for the device. Event loops send file I/O to a thread pool (next lessons) or use io_uring.

Each registration costs kernel memory: epoll(7) says roughly 160 bytes per watched descriptor on a 64-bit kernel, so 10,000 sockets take about 1.6 MB. The per-user cap `/proc/sys/fs/epoll/max_user_watches` defaults to 4 percent of low memory divided by that cost. On a 64-bit machine with 16 GiB of RAM (all of it counts as low memory there) the man page's estimate gives roughly 4 million watches (the exact default depends on the kernel's real per-item size and usable RAM).

blocks.question: A loop calls epoll_wait(ep, evs, 64, -1). 200 sockets are ready. What happens to the 136 that do not fit?
options: They are dropped and will not be reported again until new data arrives
They stay ready; later epoll_wait calls round-robin through them
epoll_wait fails with EINVAL because maxevents is too small
The kernel grows the evs array to 200 entries
blocks.explain: maxevents only limits how many entries one call copies out. The epoll_wait(2) notes say successive calls round-robin through the ready set, precisely so a few busy descriptors cannot starve the rest.

blocks.question: Why can epoll_wait cost O(ready) while poll costs O(watched)?
options: epoll uses a faster hash function for file descriptors
epoll caches socket data in user space
The kernel keeps the interest set between calls and a per-socket callback adds an item to the ready list when its state changes
epoll checks only the first 1024 descriptors
blocks.explain: poll is stateless: each call re-sends and re-scans everything. epoll is stateful: registration happens once with epoll_ctl, and readiness is pushed onto a ready list by a wait-queue callback at the moment it happens. epoll_wait only drains that list.

lessons.title: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN

blocks.md: epoll can report readiness in two ways. **Level-triggered** (LT, the default) reports a descriptor on every `epoll_wait` for as long as the condition holds: while unread bytes sit in the buffer, the socket keeps being reported. It has the same semantics as poll. **Edge-triggered** (ET, set with the `EPOLLET` flag) reports only when the state *changes*, for example when a new chunk of data arrives. The terms come from hardware interrupts: a level signal stays high, an edge is the moment it rises.

The epoll(7) page uses a five-step example with a pipe. Its read end `rfd` is registered, a writer writes 2 kB, the reader calls `epoll_wait`, reads only 1 kB, then calls `epoll_wait` again. Watch both modes side by side.

blocks.title: The epoll(7) pipe example, LT and ET

scenes.caption: Step 1: rfd is added to the interest list. The pipe is empty, so neither mode has anything to report.
Step 2: the writer puts 2048 bytes into the pipe. For ET this arrival is the edge that generates an event.
Step 3: epoll_wait returns rfd in both modes. In ET mode this consumes the event that step 2 created.
Step 4: the reader reads 1024 bytes and stops. 1024 bytes are still queued. Nothing new arrived, so there is no new edge.
Step 5: LT sees 1024 unread bytes and returns rfd again. ET saw no change since step 3, so epoll_wait may block forever while data sits in the buffer and the peer waits for a reply.

blocks.md: So the man page gives two rules for edge-triggered use: use **nonblocking** descriptors, and wait for the next event **only after** `read` or `write` has returned `EAGAIN`. Until you see `EAGAIN`, assume the descriptor is still ready. For stream sockets and pipes, a short read (fewer bytes than you asked for) also proves the buffer is empty, which saves the final call.

blocks.title: Draining an edge-triggered socket

scenes.caption: One edge event arrived; 2500 bytes are queued. The first read takes 1024.
Still ready, so read again: another 1024 bytes.
The third read gets only 452 bytes. On a stream socket this short read already proves the buffer is empty.
The fourth read fails with EAGAIN: drained. Now it is safe to return to epoll_wait. Total: 4 reads, or 3 if you trust the short read on a stream socket.
scenes.output: consumed 2500 bytes in 3 reads, then EAGAIN

blocks.md: Why choose ET at all? LT is forgiving but reports every still-ready descriptor on every wait. The classic trap is `EPOLLOUT`: a socket's send buffer usually has room, so in LT mode a socket registered for `EPOLLOUT` with nothing to send is reported on every call and the loop spins. LT code therefore adds `EPOLLOUT` with `EPOLL_CTL_MOD` only while output is pending. With ET, epoll(7) notes you can register `EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT` once and skip those MOD calls.

Draining one busy descriptor to `EAGAIN` can starve the others, since a fast sender may never let the buffer empty. epoll(7) suggests keeping your own ready list: mark the connection ready, process a bounded chunk, and round-robin across all ready connections before waiting again.

More flags worth knowing, all from [epoll_ctl(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/epoll_ctl.2.html):

- `EPOLLONESHOT`: after one event the descriptor is disabled until you re-arm it with `EPOLL_CTL_MOD`. Useful when several threads share one epoll instance, so two threads never handle the same connection at once.
- `EPOLLRDHUP`: the peer closed or shut down its writing half. Handy in ET code to detect shutdown.
- `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` (Linux 4.5): when several epoll instances watch the same descriptor, such as one listening socket, wake one or more of them instead of all, to avoid a thundering herd.

Closing a descriptor removes it from the interest list only when **every** descriptor referring to the same open file is closed. If a `dup` or a `fork` left another copy open, events can keep arriving for a number you already closed. Call `EPOLL_CTL_DEL` before closing when duplicates may exist.

Level-triggered asks "is it ready now?" on every wait. Edge-triggered says "it just became ready" once. With ET you own the state: read or write until `EAGAIN`, or remember that the connection is still ready.

blocks.question: An ET server reads one 4096-byte chunk per event and then returns to epoll_wait. A client uploads 10,000 bytes in one burst and waits for a reply. What happens?
options: The server reads all 10,000 bytes over three wakeups
epoll_wait returns EAGAIN
The kernel splits the burst into three separate edge events
The server reads 4096 bytes and may never be woken for the remaining 5904, so the client hangs
blocks.explain: Once all the bytes are queued, nothing new arrives after the first 4096 are read, so there is no new edge, and epoll_wait can block forever with 5904 bytes in the buffer. This is exactly step 5 of the epoll(7) example. Fix: read until EAGAIN, or until a short read on a stream socket.

blocks.question: A level-triggered server registers every connection with EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT and leaves it that way. CPU sits at 100 percent even with no traffic. Why?
options: EPOLLOUT is invalid without EPOLLET
Idle sockets almost always have send-buffer space, so each one is reported writable on every epoll_wait and the loop never sleeps
epoll_wait ignores the timeout when EPOLLOUT is set
The kernel rescans the interest list on every call
blocks.explain: Level-triggered means "report while the condition holds". Writable is true for nearly every idle socket, so every wait returns immediately with work that is not real. Register EPOLLOUT only while you have unsent data (EPOLL_CTL_MOD), or use ET.

lessons.title: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools

blocks.md: An event loop wraps epoll in a few more ideas: **timers**, work that cannot use readiness, and wakeups from other threads. [libuv](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/design.html), the C library under Node.js, is a well documented example. It polls nonblocking sockets with the best mechanism on each platform: epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and the BSDs, event ports on SunOS, and IOCP on Windows (a completion-based API: it reports finished operations rather than readiness).

blocks.title: One iteration of the libuv loop

scenes.caption: Pending callbacks: I/O callbacks that the previous iteration deferred run first. Then idle and prepare handles run (prepare runs right before blocking).
The loop decides how long it may sleep: 0 if there is immediate work, otherwise until the nearest timer is due, or forever if there are no timers.
Poll: the thread blocks in epoll_wait for at most that timeout, then runs the callbacks of the I/O handles whose sockets became ready.
Check handles run right after polling (Node runs setImmediate callbacks here), then close callbacks for handles closed with uv_close.
The loop updates its notion of now and runs timers that are due. If the loop still has active handles or requests, it starts the next iteration; otherwise uv_run returns.

blocks.tex: \text{timeout} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{stopping, nothing active, idle handles, or handles closing} \\ \min_i (t_i^{\text{due}}) - \text{now} & \text{if any timer is active} \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The poll timeout rules from the libuv design overview. Timers need no extra kernel object: the loop just sleeps no longer than the next deadline.

blocks.md: The loop is **one thread running one callback at a time**. Every callback runs to completion before the loop can poll again, so a slow callback delays every other client and every timer. Node's guide "Don't Block the Event Loop" puts it as: Node is fast when the work for each client at any given time is small, and fair scheduling is now *your* job, because the OS no longer preempts one client in favor of another.

blocks.title: One slow callback delays everything behind it

scenes.caption: epoll_wait returns 3 ready sockets at t = 0. Each callback takes 2 ms, the loop sleeps until the timer deadline and runs it on time at 10 ms.
Callback B parses a large request body for 40 ms. C waits until 42 ms, and the timer due at 10 ms runs at 44 ms: 34 ms late. Every other connection waits too.

Partitioned: B does 10 ms of work, then schedules the rest with setImmediate. C now finishes at 14 ms and the timer runs at 24 ms. Simplified: assumes one chunk per check phase and ignores other phases.
Simplified model: one wakeup returns k events and each callback costs c ms, so the last one waits (k - 1) x c. At k = 100 and c = 1 ms that is 99 ms.
With only 10 events per wakeup the same 1 ms callbacks add at most 9 ms. Latency on an event loop depends on how much work arrives together, not only on the slowest request.
At 200 events and 5 ms each the last callback waits 995 ms. Keeping c small (microseconds, not milliseconds) is what lets one loop serve many clients.

blocks.md:
Some work cannot be made nonblocking. Disk files have no readiness (see the lesson on epoll internals), and `getaddrinfo` is a blocking library call. libuv runs these on a **thread pool**: filesystem operations, DNS lookups (`getaddrinfo`, `getnameinfo`) and user work queued with `uv_queue_work`. The pool is global, shared by all loops, has **4 threads by default**, and can be resized at startup with the `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` environment variable up to 1024. Node also runs async `crypto.pbkdf2`, `crypto.scrypt` and zlib calls on it.

When a worker finishes, it must wake the loop thread. On Linux libuv does that with an [eventfd](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/eventfd.2.html): a kernel counter whose descriptor sits in the epoll interest list and becomes readable when another thread writes to it.

blocks.title: 8 file reads of 10 ms each on the libuv pool

scenes.caption: Simplified model: 8 independent 10 ms reads submitted at once finish in ceil(8 / workers) rounds of 10 ms. With the default 4 threads that is 2 rounds, 20 ms, even though the loop thread is idle.

blocks.md: To use more cores, run **several loops, one per thread**: the libuv loop is not thread-safe. Connections then need spreading across loops. `SO_REUSEPORT` (Linux 3.9) lets each thread own its own listening socket on the same port, which [socket(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/socket.7.html) says distributes `accept` load better than one accepting thread or many threads competing on one socket. Alternatively all loops share one listener registered with `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE`, which nginx supports. A readiness loop still pays one system call per read or write; io_uring, covered in its own course, replaces that with shared submission and completion rings.

An event loop scales because idle connections cost only a kernel watch and a small struct, and readiness is pushed to a ready list instead of scanned. It stays fast only if every callback is short: push disk I/O, DNS and CPU-heavy work to a pool, and split long jobs into chunks.

blocks.question: A Node service handles 4 slow password hashes (crypto.pbkdf2, about 100 ms each) at the same moment that 4 requests call fs.readFile. With the default pool, what do the file reads experience?
options: They queue behind the hashes on the 4-thread pool, so they finish roughly 100 ms later than they otherwise would
Nothing, file reads use epoll and never touch the pool
They run on the loop thread and block it
Node starts 4 extra threads automatically for file I/O
blocks.explain: Both async pbkdf2 and fs calls run on libuv's shared thread pool, which has 4 threads by default. The hashes occupy all 4, so the file reads wait about one hash duration. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE or moving hashing elsewhere fixes it. Disk files cannot use epoll at all.

blocks.question: The only active timer is due in 250 ms, no idle handles are active and nothing is closing. What timeout does libuv pass to the poll step?
options: 0, so it can check the timer often
-1 (infinite), since timers are handled separately
250 ms: sleep until the nearest timer is due unless I/O arrives first
10 ms, a fixed tick
blocks.explain: The libuv rules give 0 only when the loop is stopping, has nothing active, has idle handles, or is closing handles. Otherwise the timeout is the time until the closest timer, and infinity only when there are no timers. The I/O wait and the timer wait are one blocking call.

blocks.question: A team runs one libuv loop and wants to use 8 cores. Which plan matches libuv's design?
options: Call uv_run on the same loop from 8 threads
Run 8 loops in 8 threads, each with its own listening socket via SO_REUSEPORT
Set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 so network I/O spreads across threads
Register the listening socket 8 times in one epoll instance
blocks.explain: A libuv loop must be tied to one thread and is not thread-safe, so you run one loop per thread. The thread pool only runs file, DNS and queued work; network I/O stays on each loop's thread. SO_REUSEPORT gives each loop its own listener on the shared port.
